summary: Learners aged 11–12 design a full, hypothesis-led investigation (KS3 / NGSS SEP 3): a testable hypothesis with a mechanism ('because…'), named independent/dependent/≥3 control variables, planned repeats and sample size, and a hazard-with-control-measure risk assessment. The core is coordinating this design with the epistemic distinction between validity (controlling variables so the IV's effect is what is measured) and reliability (consistency across repeats). The proposed primary approach is a design-and-run studio in which poor design is intended to produce visibly untrustworthy data; supporting approaches include variable/hypothesis classification tasks and a Socratic supervisor dialogue.
misconceptions: Writing a hypothesis as a bare prediction with no 'because' / mechanism, or as a non-testable statement of opinion.
Confusing independent and dependent variables, or mislabelling a control variable as the independent variable.
Treating 'repeat three times' as a rule without understanding that repeats and sample size exist to improve reliability and expose anomalies.
Naming only one or two obvious control variables and missing subtler confounds that would invalidate the result.
Seeing risk assessment as a bureaucratic add-on rather than an integral part of designing a valid, safe investigation.
Thinking a hypothesis that turns out wrong means the investigation failed — a refuted hypothesis is a valid, informative result.

activities.title: Design studio: build it, then run it
steps: Write a testable hypothesis in the form 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because [scientific reasoning]', e.g. 'I predict warmer water will speed up dissolving BECAUSE particles move faster and collide more often'.
Assign the independent variable, the dependent variable, and name at least three control variables, justifying for each why it would otherwise affect the DV.
Before running, sketch the predicted IV–DV relationship as a graph showing the expected pattern.
Set the number of repeat readings and the sample size.
Complete a risk-assessment grid: hazard | who/what is at risk | control measure.
Run the planned (simulated) investigation and inspect the data it returns, comparing it with your predicted-results sketch.
Deliberately leave one control out (e.g. don't fix water volume), re-run, and compare how interpretable the results are.
Run a single trial versus many repeats and watch how an anomaly affects the mean.
activities.insight: Validity and reliability are properties you build into a plan: an uncontrolled variable makes results muddied and unattributable (a validity problem), while too few repeats let one anomaly swing the mean (a reliability problem). More repeats do NOT rescue a confounded design.

activities.title: Sort, judge and match (variable and hypothesis practice)
steps: For an acid-concentration-affects-reaction-rate scenario (e.g. hydrochloric acid reacting with marble chips), sort the quantities (concentration, rate/time, temperature, volume, surface area, same apparatus) into independent / dependent / control.

From several hypotheses — including the bare prediction 'more concentration = faster' and the reasoned 'increasing concentration will increase the rate BECAUSE more particles per volume means more frequent collisions' — choose which are both testable AND carry scientific reasoning, and say what is wrong with the rest.
Match named hazards to appropriate control measures.
Set repeats/sample size for the scenario and justify the choice (spotting anomalies, enabling a mean, reducing the effect of random error).
activities.insight: Variable roles, hypothesis quality, hazard control and sample-size adequacy can each be judged against clear criteria; a hypothesis needs a mechanism, and a control is something that would otherwise affect the DV.

activities.title: Supervisor challenge dialogue
steps: Present a hypothesis and plan to a lab-supervisor persona.
Respond to Socratic challenges: 'Is that testable?', 'What else could affect your DV?', 'Is three repeats enough — and what does that fix?', 'Are your results valid, reliable, or both?'.
Revise the 'because' clause and the control-variable list in response to the questioning.
activities.insight: Pressure-testing the reasoning behind a hypothesis and hunting for subtler confounds can strengthen the 'because' clause and surface missed controls.

checkQuestion: You're planning an experiment on whether the concentration of a sugar solution affects how fast a reaction happens. Talk me through your full plan: your hypothesis and the reasoning behind it, which variable you change, which you measure, at least three you must control, and how many readings or repeats you'd take and why. Then explain the difference between making your results VALID and making them RELIABLE.
checkAnswer: A strong plan states a reasoned hypothesis ('increasing concentration will increase the rate BECAUSE more particles per volume means more frequent collisions'), correctly assigns the independent variable (concentration) and dependent variable (rate/time), names at least three genuine controls (temperature, volume, same apparatus, surface area…), plans repeats (e.g. three runs, take a mean) and an adequate sample, and identifies hazards with control measures. Crucially it distinguishes VALIDITY (controlling variables so the test actually measures the effect of the IV) from RELIABILITY (consistency across repeats), and treats the hypothesis as a testable prediction with a mechanism, not a guess.
